title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7.

checks.explanation: Autosomal dominant inheritance linked to SCN9A mutation implies heterozygous mutation; the case mutation is also explicitly heterozygous.

checks.explanation: The paper says SCN9A encodes Nav1.7. Calling it 'voltage-gated sodium channel' is standard nomenclature, and the abstract calls it a sodium channel.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, previously known as familial rectal pain, is an inherited condition characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing (Fertleman et al., 2006). Onset is in the neonatal period or infancy and the disorder persists throughout life; autonomic manifestations predominate early, and attacks of excruciating deep burning pain characterize the later course (Fertleman et al., 2007). The disorder is a sodium channelopathy caused by mutation in SCN9A (Fertleman et al., 2006).

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) described the clinical phenotype in 77 individuals from 15 families identified through an international consortium; a validated pain questionnaire was completed by 14 affected individuals. Onset was in the neonatal period or infancy, and the disorder persisted throughout life. Autonomic manifestations predominated initially, with skin flushing in all and harlequin color change and tonic attacks in most. Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia and sometimes asystole were common. Later, the disorder was characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas, but also diffuse. Attacks were triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2006) noted that other SCN9A mutations, associated with more negative activation thresholds, cause primary erythermalgia. Carbamazepine, which is effective in PEPD but not in primary erythermalgia, selectively blocked the persistent current associated with PEPD mutants but did not affect the negative activation threshold of a primary erythermalgia mutant. The authors concluded that PEPD and primary erythermalgia are allelic disorders with distinct underlying biophysical mechanisms.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-year-old girl with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder manifesting as extremely painful voiding since birth, Meglič et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.554G-A transition in the SCN9A gene, resulting in an arg185-to-his (R185H) substitution. The mutation was inherited from her father, who had occasionally had pain in his jaw while yawning since childhood. The authors noted that the same mutation had been found in patients with small fiber sensory neuropathy. Carbamazepine significantly reduced the girl's pain.

agent.process_note: Read all 7 files in full. Four (Hayden and Grossman 1959, Dugan 1972, Mann and Cree 1972, Fertleman and Ferrie 2006) are title only, so they are cited only for what their titles say. Three are abstracts only (Fertleman et al. 2006, 2007; Meglič et al. 2014). The Fertleman et al. (2006) abstract does not name its 8 SCN9A missense mutations or give a mapped locus, so the only named allelic variant is R185H (Meglič et al., 2014). No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the SCN9A MIM number and chromosome location are left out of the intro.
